structure.title: Act I · A friend borrows against ships at sea
structure.text: Bassanio needs money to court Portia. Antonio is rich on paper but has little cash available. A loan between enemies lets the friend travel and leaves a dangerous promise behind in Venice.

structure.title: Acts II–III · Belmont and Venice · Choices with conditions
structure.text: In Belmont suitors choose among caskets according to a dead father's instructions. In Venice a daughter's departure and rumours about shipping turn old injuries into urgent business. Marriage, inheritance and credit keep passing between the two households.

structure.title: Acts IV–V · A courtroom and a return to Belmont
structure.text: In court the wording of a promise acquires frightening precision. Afterwards a smaller domestic dispute about rings brings back the question of who can demand that a promise be honoured to the letter.

people.name: Shylock and Antonio
people.text: They know one another as business competitors and as members of unequal religious communities. Antonio has insulted Shylock publicly. When audience sympathy shifts, that history still belongs to the transaction.

people.name: Portia
people.text: She has money, wit and very definite views about her visitors. Her marriage is nonetheless governed by a test devised by her father. The resources she brings to somebody else's legal difficulty throw light on her own.

people.name: Jessica
people.text: She sees leaving home as an opening onto love and a new community. Her father experiences the same departure as bereavement, theft and betrayal. The play makes room for both accounts to be heard.

context.title: Christian power and anti-Jewish abuse
context.text: Insults, exclusion and pressure to convert belong to the ordinary conduct of people who praise mercy. A production's choices about who laughs at a joke and who stands silent during it can alter the experience of an entire scene.

notice.text: Follow an object back to the giver.
notice.why: A ring may carry a memory the next owner cannot see. What looks like a simple exchange to one person can amount to the loss of a relationship for another.
Lending a name, a purse or a legal argument can rescue a friend. Look closely at who supplies the money and who bears the danger when one person offers another a favour.

opening: Bassanio needs money to court a wealthy woman, and his friend Antonio is willing to borrow it for him. The lender, Shylock, belongs to a community Antonio despises, and proposes a penalty that sounds too grotesque to become real. Shakespeare sets the bargain beside a romantic contest in which another person's fortune is also at stake. Promises, prejudice, and calculated generosity draw the stories together, until the people most fluent in the language of mercy have to demonstrate what they mean by it.
